elements.content: Grammar focus: Stylistic Register-Switching & Tonal Control.

Core Rule: Master register control by pairing Latinate nominalisations and passive hedging in executive/academic modes with active, Anglo-Saxon idioms and direct verbs in collaborative modes.

The executive committee — deemed the proposal financially unviable .
We — need to pull back on this project because it costs too much .
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Which phrase represents an appropriate executive register for a formal briefing?
options: We must benchmark our performance against industry standards.
We gotta check out how other companies do stuff.

elements.content: 2. What distinguishes the formal academic register from informal speech?
options: Greater use of nominalisation and Latinate vocabulary
Frequent reliance on phrasal verbs and contractions

elements.content: Read and listen: three examples in context.

1. Function check: What is the primary purpose of using Stylistic Register-Switching & Tonal Control?
options: To express clear, level-appropriate meaning in structured context
To translate sentences word-for-word from another language
It is an obsolete form never used by native speakers

elements.content: 2. Form check: Does correct usage of Stylistic Register-Switching & Tonal Control require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
options: No, agreement rules are optional in English
Yes, matching grammatical forms ensures natural, accurate communication
Agreement only matters in formal academic writing
